questions.prompt: Put the core auth loop (login → issue → validate → refresh → revoke) in order.
steps: The client sends username and password to the auth server
The auth server verifies the credentials against the hashed password in the DB
The auth server issues an access token and a refresh token
The client calls the resource API with `Authorization: Bearer <access_token>`
The API middleware validates the JWT signature and claims
When the access token expires, the client calls `/auth/refresh` with the refresh token
On logout or breach detection, the refresh token is revoked
questions.explanation: This single loop is most of every auth server; RS256, JWKS, rotation and reuse detection are hardening around it.

source.section: Before any code, understand the shape of the system. There are always 3 parties:

questions.prompt: How do the access token and the refresh token differ?
options: The access token is long-lived and sent only to `/auth/refresh`; the refresh token is short-lived and sent to every API
The refresh token is the user's password, encrypted
They are identical tokens with different names
The access token is a short-lived JWT that proves identity to APIs; the refresh token is long-lived and used only to get a new access token
questions.explanation: Access tokens are short-lived (e.g. 15 minutes) and go to the APIs; refresh tokens last days or weeks and are only exchanged at the refresh endpoint.

questions.prompt: What is the auth server's `GET /.well-known/jwks.json` endpoint for?
options: Listing every user account
Exposing the public signing keys so APIs can verify RS256-signed JWTs
Issuing new refresh tokens
Returning the current user's profile
questions.explanation: JWKS publishes the public keys; APIs use them to check signatures without ever seeing the private key.

questions.prompt: A user-facing client receives both an ID token and an access token. Which one should it send to call the API?
options: The access token; ID tokens are for signing the user in and should not be used to call APIs
The ID token, because it describes the user
Both, joined with a dot
Neither; it should send the refresh token
questions.explanation: Access tokens are for API authorization; ID tokens are for signing the user in to the client.

source.section: How the developer usually builds it

questions.prompt: A background job in one backend service must call another service with no user involved. Which flow fits?
options: The authorization code flow with the user's password
Sending an ID token
The client credentials flow, using the application's own identity
Calling `/auth/refresh` with no token
questions.explanation: Service-to-service calls use the client credentials flow, which is based on the application's identity rather than a user's, common for daemons and background jobs.

source.section: How the developer usually builds it

questions.prompt: What is the main drawback of having the same Web API handle login, token issuing and business endpoints (Option 1)?
options: It cannot validate JWTs
Auth and business logic are tightly coupled, which makes it hard to scale and to reuse across multiple APIs
Clients cannot store the tokens
It requires an external identity provider
questions.explanation: Option 1 is fine for learning, small internal apps and MVPs, but production systems usually use a separate auth server that several APIs trust.

source.section: ✅ Option 1: Same API handles Auth + Tokens (Beginner / Small apps)
